title: Introduction to Generative AI and LLM APIs
why: This is the first lecture of the module. First we'll see the whole picture — what you'll build in 24 lectures, why you can't do it yet and who you'll be by the end of the module. Then we'll learn how a language model works inside: what it “reads”, how it writes an answer, why it makes mistakes and what it costs — so that from the next lecture, when we write code, these questions won't come up.
outcomes: explain what you'll build in the module, what you'll be able to do and who you'll become
explain how an LLM produces text: tokens, next-token prediction, context window
choose Temperature, Top-P and Max Tokens for the task
choose a provider and calculate the monthly cost in tokens

review.q: What is a token and why do we care about it in the backend?
review.a: a piece of text the model reads and writes in · price, the context window limit and speed are counted in tokens; Georgian — more tokens

review.q: How does an LLM write an answer?
review.a: next-token prediction: computes probabilities for the next token → picks one → appends it → repeats until it finishes or hits the limit

review.q: The model named the price of our dish. Why don't we trust it?
review.a: it has never seen our menu; it writes what's likely, not what's true — hallucination · prices always come from the database

review.q: Why doesn't the model “remember” the previous request?
review.a: stateless: every request is independent · we have to send the history every time

review.q: Which Temperature do we set to detect the order type, and what does `finish_reason = length` mean?
review.a: 0 — one correct answer, the same every time · length — it hit Max Tokens, the answer was cut off

review.q: The restaurant chat has 300 conversations a day. What increases the cost the most?
review.a: an expensive model (prices differ tenfold) · a growing history that is sent again every time · Georgian text — more tokens

resources.title: Tiktokenizer — text to tokens (choose gpt-4o)
resources.note: see how text splits into tokens

options: One word
A piece of text the model reads and writes in
One letter
One sentence
quiz.explain: A token can be a word, a syllable or a letter — the tokenizer decides. Price, limits and speed are counted in tokens.

quiz.q: The same idea in English and in Georgian. What happens with Georgian?
options: The tokens are the same
Many more tokens → more expensive and slower
Fewer tokens
The model can't read Georgian
quiz.explain: The tokenizer “saw” little Georgian, so a Georgian word splits into several parts.

quiz.q: How does an LLM write an answer?
options: It looks up a ready answer in a database
At every step it calculates probabilities for the next token, picks one and repeats
It writes the whole answer at once
It searches the internet for the answer
quiz.explain: This is next-token prediction — the core mechanism of an LLM.

quiz.q: The model said: “Khinkali costs 1.20 ₾ here”. What do we do?
options: Trust it — the model is smart
Set Temperature to 0 and then trust it
The price always comes from our database (tool or RAG)
Use a bigger model
quiz.explain: This is hallucination: the model writes what is likely, not what is true. Temperature 0 makes the answer consistent, not correct.

quiz.q: First request: “My name is Nino”. Second, separate request: “What's my name?”. What will it answer?
options: “Nino”
It won't know — the model is stateless
It remembers for 24 hours
Only if we write in Georgian
quiz.explain: Every request is independent. For “memory” we have to send the history every time.

quiz.q: We extract the date and party size from a customer's text. Which Temperature?
quiz.explain: There is one correct answer and we want the same result every time.

quiz.q: The response says `finish_reason: "length"`. What does it mean?
options: The model finished successfully
It hit Max Tokens — the answer was cut off
We sent a text that was too long
The model restarted
quiz.explain: A normal finish is `stop`. On `length`, raise the limit or log it.

options: Returns 90% of the text
Keeps the most likely tokens until their sum reaches 90%
Sets Temperature to 0.9
Limits the answer to 90 tokens
quiz.explain: It cuts the weak “tail”, and the choice happens only among the remaining tokens.

quiz.q: FAQ bot: “Open on Sunday?”. Should we use a reasoning model?
options: Yes — it's always better
No — it's a simple question; reasoning is slow and we pay for thinking tokens
Yes, if it's in Georgian
Only in the evening, when the load is low
quiz.explain: Reasoning is worth it for multi-step tasks, not simple questions.

quiz.q: 10M input and 1M output tokens a month. Price: $0.15 / $0.60 (per 1M). Cost?
When is a local model (running on our own server) the better choice?
options: When we want the strongest model
When customer data must not leave the company
When we want good quality in Georgian
When we don't have a server
quiz.explain: A local model keeps the data inside the system; on the other hand, it needs a powerful server and small models are weak in Georgian.

quiz.q: Where do we store the Gemini API key?
options: In `appsettings.json`
In code, as a const
In the environment variable `GEMINI_API_KEY`
In `launchSettings.json`
quiz.explain: The other files go to Git — bots find a leaked key within minutes.

summary: In this module an **AI agent** appears in your API: the model decides what to do, and **your C# code** does it.
The model reads text as **tokens** and sees only numbers. Price, limits and speed are counted in tokens; Georgian takes more tokens.
The model writes the **likely** next token, not the true one. Prices, stock and reservations must always come **from the database**.
The model **doesn't remember** the previous request: we send the history every time, and we pay for it.
**Temperature**, **Top-P** and **Max Tokens** are set per request, depending on the task. Cost = tokens × price, and output is more expensive than input.
